name: Tara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Confidential is good. I'm on the women's network committee for the union, so I'm used to people being careful what they say. Go for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an underground loader at the Kestrel gold mine. After the miners fire a blast, I go in and scoop out the broken rock, the muck, and carry it to the trucks or the ore pass, which is a shaft the rock drops down. It's dark, loud, wet, and I love it more than I expected. I'm still slow lining up the bucket on a tight drive, and the old hands tease me about it. What wears me out is the hour at the end of shift waiting for the cage to take us up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine by me. We've already got tele-remote loaders on a couple of levels, where someone drives from a chair on the surface, so I'd say the robots were never about the clever AI stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. I'm only two years in and I've just started feeling competent. I'd like a few more years of being bad at this before a machine is better at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, get my tickets for the bigger loader, and keep doing my union stuff. Maybe I'd finally use that AI app properly to help write the women's network newsletter, because it takes me forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the picture where I get to just learn my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned tele-remote loaders. Who drives those at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of the senior operators, Priya and Craig, from a room up top. They say it's boring and their backs hurt less. I've watched over Priya's shoulder a few times and it looks like a video game with real consequences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to do that one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, once I'm good at the real thing. I think you need to have felt the bucket hit the rock before you can do it from a screen.

S0.say: I'd say that's fine by me, because the robots underground were never about clever AI anyway. We already have tele-remote loaders driven from the surface on a couple of levels.
S0.think: Privately it's a relief, because I've only just started feeling competent after two years. I'd like a few more years of learning before a machine is better at it.
S0.do: Keeps working towards her ticket for the bigger loader and keeps up her union work. Might start using an AI app now and then to help write the union women's network newsletter.
S0.feel: Calm, like she finally gets to just learn her job.
S0.quote: I'd like a few more years of being bad at this before a machine is better at it.
S0.fieldNote: She already lives next to automation through the tele-remote loaders, so this picture holds no shock. She wants to master the hands-on job before moving to a screen. Her humour about being bad at the job hides real pride in getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table on how it's rolled out. Change is fine, but who decides the pace and who gets trained matters. I'd post about it in the network group, and probably get into an argument with my cousin who thinks unions are dinosaurs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means more tele-remote, faster, and fewer people underground. That's actually safer, which I can't argue with. But it also means fewer jobs, and I'm not senior enough to be first pick for the screen jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote course as soon as it opened, even before I'm good on the real loader. I'd push the union to make the training open to juniors, not just the old hands. And I'd keep my savings where they are, about four months, rather than spend on the trip Dev and I had planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's the kind of change I can see a path through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's safer and you can't argue with that. Has safety been personal for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year a rock fall on level eleven buried a loader bucket. No one was in it because it was on remote that shift. I went and looked at that bucket afterwards and thought, that could've been my lunchbox on the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So do you want more remote or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, which is annoying. I want more of it for safety and less of it for my job. That's why I think the union has to be in the room, so it's not just one or the other.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table on how automation is rolled out, who decides the pace and who gets trained. I'd post about it in the network group.
S1.think: Privately I think it means more tele-remote and fewer people underground, which is safer. But fewer jobs too, and I'm not senior enough to be first pick.
S1.do: Puts her name down for the tele-remote course as soon as it opens and pushes the union to open training to juniors. Holds onto her four months of savings instead of spending on a planned trip.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, but she can see a path through.
S1.quote: I went and looked at that bucket afterwards and thought, that could've been my lunchbox on the seat.
S1.fieldNote: She is torn in an honest way: automation saved a colleague's life last year and could also take her job. She would move towards tele-remote once it's proven, not before. Her trip with her partner was the first thing she'd shelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an emergency and the government has to act like it. Public money for wages while people retrain, rules on how fast mines can cut, and a share of the profits for the towns. I'd be at the rally with a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd lose the job and so would Dev, eventually, if robots can frame a house. Two years is no time. My savings would last four months and then what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Dev and work out what we can cut and put every spare dollar into savings. I'd go hard with the union and the network on a transition deal, and I'd call my local member every week if I had to. If I lost the job I'd apply for whatever support there was, without shame, because that's what it's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It's the first time in this interview I've felt my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum worked thirty years at the cannery and lost that job when it closed. She'd say, I told you not to go underground, and then she'd ask if we need money, which she doesn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd move to tele-remote once it was proven. Does that still work here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the thing. If AI can drive the loader with no one watching, the screen job goes too. My whole plan was one step behind the machines, and in this picture there's no step.

S2.say: I'd say this is an emergency and the government must act like it: public money for wages during retraining, limits on how fast mines can cut, and a profit share for towns.
S2.think: Privately I think she and her partner would both lose their work if robots can frame houses too. Two years is no time and her savings only last four months.
S2.do: Sits down with her partner in the first month to cut costs and save every spare dollar. Campaigns hard through the union and her local member for a transition deal, and takes government support without shame if laid off.
S2.feel: Frightened, with her stomach dropping for the first time in the interview.
S2.quote: She'd say, I told you not to go underground, and then she'd ask if we need money, which she doesn't have.
S2.fieldNote: She noticed for herself that her careful plan to move to tele-remote collapses in this picture. Her mother's job loss at a cannery is a strong background memory. She treats public support as a right, not a shame, which fits her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's not waste them. Every mine should have a transition plan on the table now, worked out with the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to get one solid trade, if I start straight away. Not enough to wait around and see. My worry is I'd sit on my hands for two years like everyone else and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within six months I'd apply for an electrical apprenticeship. Electricians install and fix all the gear, including the robots, so it buys time. I'd take the pay cut, use savings to cover the gap, and keep up the union work on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship is a big pay cut. How would you and Dev manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to put off buying a place, probably three or four years. Dev wouldn't love it, but he did an apprenticeship himself, so he gets it. We'd be back to two-minute noodles at twenty-eight, which is a weird thing to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electricians fix the robots. What if robots fix robots, by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I thought of that while I said it. Maybe it just buys me five more years. But five more years of a wage is five more years, and I'd rather be near the machines than far from them.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years so let's not waste them, and every mine should have a transition plan on the table now, worked out with the workers.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough for one solid trade if she starts at once, but not enough to wait and see. She worries she'd sit on her hands like everyone else.
S3.do: Applies for an electrical apprenticeship within six months and uses savings to cover the pay cut. Delays buying a home with her partner by three or four years and keeps up union work.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy with it, which she feels she can handle.
S3.quote: We'd be back to two-minute noodles at twenty-eight, which is a weird thing to choose.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she turns from campaigning to a concrete personal move: an electrical apprenticeship. She caught the weakness in her own plan, that robots may fix robots, and accepted it as buying time. Delaying the home purchase is the real cost she named.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to make it fair: shorter weeks, retraining, the profits shared. I'd want the union pushing for a four-day week rather than layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can finish learning this job and still have time to switch. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's young. I think I'd be all right, as long as I don't get lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd honestly keep going on the loader and do the tele-remote course. Around year three I'd start the electrical apprenticeship. I'd keep saving a bit each month and probably do a short course on the AI tools, since Priya says the new systems are all screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, but more like nervous before a test than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a four-day week. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. But if the robots do the work, someone has to explain why the gain goes to shareholders and not to us. A four-day week is the easiest thing to explain at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably keep the plan to buy a place in two years. Kids maybe later. With ten years, I'd let myself think about a future that isn't just survival.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should use it to make the change fair, with shorter weeks, retraining and shared profits. I'd want the union pushing for a four-day week.
S4.think: Privately ten years lets me finish learning this job and still switch. At thirty-seven I'd be young, and I'd be fine as long as I didn't get lazy.
S4.do: Keeps running the loader and takes the tele-remote course in the first year, then starts an electrical apprenticeship around year three. Saves a bit each month and does a short course on AI tools.
S4.feel: Nervous like before a test, not scared.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd let myself think about a future that isn't just survival.
S4.fieldNote: Time turns her from defensive to hopeful, and she started talking about kids for the first time. She was frank that she doesn't know whether a four-day week is realistic. Her plan stages the change, which fits her habit of moving once things are proven.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no room to do the sensible thing. What would help is wage support while people retrain, and training that's open to juniors, not handed out by seniority.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask women specifically. There are only six of us underground at Kestrel. It took us ten years to get in the door, and I'd hate for the door to close right behind us.

headlineQuote: It took us ten years to get in the door, and I'd hate for the door to close right behind us.
portrait: Tara Petrov is 27 and runs an underground loader at the Kestrel gold mine, two years in and still slow lining up the bucket. She lives with her partner Dev, a carpenter, has about four months saved, and sits on her union's women's network committee. She is open to change once it's proven and already watches tele-remote loaders at work. She stays calm in the plateau picture, gets frightened by AGI in two years because her step-behind-the-machines plan collapses, and with five or ten years moves towards an electrical apprenticeship while campaigning for a fair transition.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to do the sensible thing like learning a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support while people retrain, and training places open to juniors rather than handed out by seniority.
